assessments.quantum_threat: Designed to resist known quantum attacks; not proven secure
assessments.recommendation: NIST-standardized post-quantum algorithm (NIST category 3). Confirm the implementation is validated and maintained, and watch for side-channel and protocol-integration issues. Standardization is not a proof of security.

This algorithm is not yet present in the Q-SOC assessment table. Add a mapping entry in app/quantum/crypto_assessment.py after consulting authoritative sources before treating this as a real classification.

This algorithm is not yet present in the Q-SOC assessment table. Add a mapping entry in app/quantum/crypto_assessment.py after consulting authoritative sources before treating this as a real classification.

As with symmetric ciphers, Grover's algorithm offers a theoretical quadratic speedup for preimage search against hash functions, reducing (not eliminating) the effective security margin. SHA-256 remains widely used; monitor NIST guidance for updates.

Grover's algorithm does not 'break' AES; under the idealized quantum-search model it reduces the effective brute-force security strength (roughly by half, in exponent terms). Consider AES-256 for a larger theoretical safety margin where practical.

assessments.migration_status: More Suitable Against Theoretical Quantum Search Threat
assessments.recommendation: AES-256 retains a substantial theoretical security margin under Grover's quadratic speedup model and is generally considered a reasonable symmetric choice for long-term data protection.
Evaluate ML-KEM (FIPS 203) for key establishment, commonly in a hybrid with ECDH during the transition.
Larger key size does not resolve the theoretical quantum vulnerability of RSA. Plan migration to a post-quantum mechanism appropriate to the use case.
Evaluate ML-DSA (FIPS 204) or SLH-DSA (FIPS 205) for signatures; FN-DSA (FIPS 206) is not final.

Plan migration to a post-quantum key-establishment/signature mechanism (e.g. ML-KEM for key establishment, ML-DSA or SLH-DSA for signatures) as a migration candidate based on use case. Not a universal replacement.

extra.note: Educational toy demonstration. This experiment factors the small example N=15 using a real quantum order-finding circuit plus classical post-processing; it does not break real-world RSA.

Educational demonstration of Grover's algorithm on a 2-qubit search space. One Grover iteration amplifies the marked state's measurement probability; results come from real circuit execution, not fabricated data.

scenarios.name: Authentication failure burst
scenarios.description: 12 failed logins from one source IP within ~1 minute.
scenarios.cleanup: No cleanup required -- synthetic events only, no host-level side effects.
scenarios.lab_instructions: On YOUR OWN enrolled lab VM only, make 12 failed SSH password attempts as a non-existent user from another lab machine you own (for example: for i in $(seq 12); do ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=password nosuchuser@<lab-vm>; done, entering a wrong password). The enrolled agent ships the resulting auth.log lines. Then click Evaluate. Do not do this against any machine you do not own or administer.

rules.name: Brute-force-like login burst
rules.description: A fast burst of authentication failures from the same source IP (default 10 in 5 minutes).

mitre.rationale: A fast burst of failures from one source matches online brute force.

rules.name: Privilege-related authentication activity
rules.description: A privilege-use or privilege-escalation-flagged authentication event.

mitre.rationale: Privilege use by an account is associated with valid-account abuse but is also routine admin activity.

rules.name: Repeated failed logins
rules.description: Authentication failures from the same source IP reaching a threshold within a window (default 5 in 10 minutes).

mitre.rationale: Repeated failed authentication from one source is the guessing behaviour T1110 describes.

rules.name: Successful login after multiple failures
rules.description: A successful authentication from a source IP that had several failures in the preceding window (default 3 in 10 minutes).

mitre.rationale: A success after failures may mean guessed credentials now give valid-account access; it cannot be proven from logs alone.

rules.name: Data access anomaly
rules.description: Indicator rule: fires on an event typed data_access_anomaly.

mitre.rationale: Anomalous access to local data stores (previously T1530, which is specific to cloud storage).

rules.name: Persistence indicator
rules.description: Indicator rule: fires on an event typed persistence_indicator.

mitre.rationale: Persistence indicator associated with autostart mechanisms; the specific mechanism depends on the upstream source.

rules.name: Privilege escalation indicator
rules.description: Indicator rule: fires on an event typed privilege_escalation_indicator.

mitre.rationale: Generic indicator; the tactic is known but no specific technique (e.g. T1068 exploitation) is evidenced.

rules.name: Ransomware-like file activity burst
rules.description: Several suspicious file-activity events on one host within a window (default 5 in 2 minutes). In the simulator this is synthetic telemetry only.

mitre.rationale: A burst of file-modification events resembles ransomware encryption. In the simulator this is synthetic telemetry only.

rules.name: Suspicious file activity
rules.description: Indicator rule: a single event typed suspicious_file_activity.

mitre.rationale: A single generic file-activity flag does not evidence data manipulation (previously T1565).

rules.name: Suspicious process event
rules.description: Indicator rule: fires on an event typed suspicious_process (relies on the upstream sensor's classification).

mitre.rationale: Fires on a generic 'suspicious process' flag (previously T1055 Process Injection, which is far more specific than the evidence).

rules.name: Repeated connection attempts
rules.description: Many connection attempts from one source IP within a window (default 20 in 5 minutes).

mitre.rationale: High connection volume alone does not evidence a specific technique (previously mapped to T1071, which concerns command-and-control protocols; that was not defensible).

rules.name: Synthetic port-scan pattern
rules.description: Connection attempts from one source IP to many distinct destination ports (default 8 ports in 2 minutes).

mitre.rationale: Many distinct destination ports from one source in a short window is port scanning for services.

rules.name: Unexpected service access
rules.description: An event explicitly flagged as access to an unexpected/unauthorized service.

mitre.rationale: Fires on a generic upstream flag; exploitation of the service (T1210) is not evidenced.

rules.name: Threat-intel indicator match
rules.description: An event field matched an enabled, unexpired indicator of compromise (IP, domain, URL or file hash). Matches against TEST indicators are labelled as such and are not evidence of malicious activity.

mitre.rationale: An indicator match says an observable was seen; it does not by itself identify an ATT&CK technique.

rules.name: Abnormal API request rate
rules.description: API request volume from one source IP above a threshold (default 50 in 1 minute).

mitre.rationale: A request flood may be an application-layer DoS, but could equally be a misbehaving client or scraping.

rules.name: Repeated API authentication failures
rules.description: API authentication failures from one source IP reaching a threshold (default 5 in 5 minutes).

mitre.rationale: Repeated authentication failures against an API from one source.

rules.name: Suspicious web request pattern
rules.description: An event explicitly flagged as a suspicious/common-web-attack-indicator request pattern.

mitre.rationale: Request patterns resembling common web-attack indicators against a public-facing application.
